149.12400,-35.30800.name: OGTR — consultation on licence applications
149.12400,-35.30800.state: Canberra — Department of Health, Scarborough House
149.12400,-35.30800.desc: Publishes each application, the risk assessment and risk management plan, and the proposed field sites, which few regulators publish before a decision, then invites comment for around thirty days. Knowing the sites before the decision is what makes a local objection possible at all, and few regulators provide it at that stage — though EU member states do publish trial locations under the deliberate release directive.

149.12400,-35.30800.name: Gene Technology Amendment Regulations 2019 and FSANZ P1055 — Australia's carve-out
149.12400,-35.30800.desc: The map holds nineteen Australian records, including two on the Gene Technology Regulator praising it as one of the few regulators that publishes field trial coordinates before a decision. None recorded what that regulator no longer sees. Amendments to the Gene Technology Regulations 2001, notified 4 April 2019 and in effect from October, revised the schedule of organisms that are not GMOs: an SDN-1 edit, where a site-directed nuclease is used with NO REPAIR TEMPLATE and no foreign DNA remains, is outside the definition. SDN-2, which uses an artificially created template, stays inside it. The food side followed separately: FSANZ Proposal P1055, opened February 2020 with two public consultations and 1,736 submissions on the first, replaced the process-based definition with a new definition of genetically modified food including a list of exemptions and a definition of null segregant. FSANZ's own account names the alignment: Canada, Japan and England. So the regulator whose transparency this map holds up as a standard publishes trial locations for the organisms still inside the definition, and nothing for those outside it.
